claims.text: An in-situ laser remelting pass after each deposited layer reduces residual thermal gradients in additively manufactured high-entropy alloys.
Layer-by-layer laser remelting promotes microstructural homogenization in additively manufactured high-entropy alloys.
Layer-by-layer laser remelting improves dimensional precision, including reduced warping and shrinkage, relative to conventional one-pass deposition.
Layer-by-layer laser remelting improves the mechanical integrity of additively manufactured high-entropy-alloy components.
Layer-by-layer laser remelting reduces fabrication-induced defects in additively manufactured high-entropy alloys.
As-built high-entropy-alloy components made by standard additive manufacturing exhibit residual stresses.
As-built high-entropy-alloy components made by standard additive manufacturing exhibit microporosity.
As-built additively manufactured alloys can exhibit chemical or microstructural heterogeneity.
Scanning the same consolidated layer an additional time can remelt that layer.
The added remelting pass enhances melt-pool overlap.
Thermal homogenization caused by remelting reduces porosity.
Enhanced overlap and thermal homogenization produce smoother layer interfaces.
Enhanced overlap and thermal homogenization minimize residual stresses.
Relaxation of thermal gradients during the added laser pass heals defects.
The added laser pass facilitates more uniform solidification.
Microstructural heterogeneity and nonuniform defect distributions cause dimensional distortion.
Microstructural heterogeneity and nonuniform defect distributions create mechanically weak regions.
Remelted components will have higher tensile strength, hardness, and ductility than conventionally built components.
Remelted components will have a lower density of pores and microcracks than conventionally built components.
The effectiveness of laser processing depends on the selected process parameters, while extreme energy inputs may cause over-melting or microstructural coarsening.
